executive_summary: SGD/JPY trades at 123.081 (6 August close), down 2.19% over one month, 1.43% over three months and 0.99% over six months, but still 3.93% higher over twelve. The pair's entire recent history was rewritten in two sessions: from a 52-week high of 127.089 on 26 July it collapsed 3.15% to close 31 July at 122.786, driven wholly by the yen leg after Japan intervened for roughly ¥8.45tn on 30 July and then, for the first time ever, was joined by the US Treasury on 31 July — the yen appreciated by nearly 5% over three sessions on coordinated purchases by Tokyo and Washington, with Tokyo deploying approximately 5.33 trillion yen during Friday's operations. The dominant bilateral narrative is therefore no longer the slow S$NEER grind that carried this cross higher through 2025 and H1 2026; it is a policy and official-flow asymmetry in which every catalyst with the power to move the pair sits on the Japanese side. The critical differential that neither standalone dossier surfaces is that SGD/JPY is now the only genuinely carry-neutral cross in the G10+SGD complex — SORA at 0.97% against a BoJ target of 1.00% is a −3bp annualised carry for a long position — so there is no cushion whatsoever, and a single BoJ hike to 1.25% flips the Singapore dollar into being the outright lowest-yielding currency in the set. Against that, the structural case for the pair is the strongest fiscal and external-balance gap in the entire benchmarking universe: Aaa/AAA/AAA and a 1.9%-of-GDP fiscal surplus against A1/A+/A and a 187.6%-of-GDP debt stock financed at a 29-year-high assumed rate, plus an energy terms-of-trade shock that hurts Japan roughly twice as hard as it hurts Singapore's refining-hub structure. We are tactically Bearish SGD/JPY at conviction 4 (net score −0.3637, target 121.80 over two to four weeks) and only mildly Bearish strategically at conviction 2 (net score −0.1051, target 121.00), the horizon gap reflecting genuine offsetting forces rather than indecision. The principal caveat is that intervention-led yen rallies in April–May 2026 and in 2024 both failed without a policy follow-through, and here the follow-through is a single 18 September BoJ meeting priced somewhere between 44% and "done deal" depending on whom you read.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no direct PPP series for this cross, but the two dossiers' REER-relative constructions are internally consistent and produce an unusually large number: the SGD dossier puts the Singapore dollar 7.67% rich versus the yen, and the JPY dossier puts the yen 7.7% cheap versus the Singapore dollar — the same reading from both sides, implying a REER-relative fair value near 114.1 against spot of 123.08. That gap is almost entirely a yen story: Singapore's BIS real broad REER at 114.28 sits within 0.15% of its own 30-month mean, the smallest deviation in the eleven-currency set, while Japan's at 65.30 is 7.82% below its mean and the lowest reading ever recorded on the series. This is precisely the configuration that makes official intervention politically viable and analytically defensible. What is priced at 123.08 is a permanent yen discount: OCBC projected USD/SGD drifting moderately lower toward 1.26 by year-end while consensus USD/JPY sits near 157.8 for December, which crosses to roughly 122.3 — barely below spot. The market is pricing a 7.7% real-effective dislocation to close at under 1% a year.

market_context.recent_regime: Through the first three weeks of July this was the quietest kind of trend: the pair ground from 124.7 to 127.09 on a combination of MAS's 27 July slope increase and relentless yen weakness, with daily ranges of 20–40 pips. That regime ended on 30 July when the US and Japan launched a coordinated rescue for the yen, with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York selling euros for yen on behalf of the Treasury through Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs — the first time the US had intervened to stem the yen's decline. The pair has since traded a 121.29–123.46 range while the market tests whether official flow has changed the trend or merely interrupted it. The dominant narrative for the next month is not Singaporean at all: it is whether the BoJ ratifies the intervention with a 18 September hike.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: This is the defining structural feature of SGD/JPY and it is unique in the G10+SGD complex. Singapore has no policy rate; SORA fixed at 0.97% in July, and the BoJ target is around 1.0 percent. The annualised carry on a long SGD/JPY position is therefore −3bp — the Singapore dollar is, for the first time, the lower-yielding leg. There is no carry to earn, no carry to pay and no carry cushion in either direction: this is a pure directional expression of relative policy trajectory. The trajectory is unambiguously against the pair: a single 25bp BoJ move takes the pair's carry to −28bp; two moves take it to −53bp. Singapore's SORA cannot respond, because it is an output of the S$NEER band under covered interest parity rather than an instrument, so the carry differential can only widen against a long SGD/JPY position, never in its favour, unless MAS engineers a materially steeper appreciation path. Read from the other side, a short SGD/JPY position costs essentially nothing to hold, which is the single most attractive mechanical feature of expressing a bearish yen-cross view here rather than in AUD/JPY (−335bp) or NOK/JPY (−325bp). The forward curve embeds almost nothing, meaning essentially the entire expected spot move is genuine edge rather than financed-away carry — the reverse of the situation in USD/JPY.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral money-market differential is −3bp in the yen's favour and the direction of travel is entirely one-way. MAS has no policy rate to raise; its tightening arrives as a slope adjustment estimated at 25bp to 1.25% per annum on the S$NEER, which is a trade-weighted rate of appreciation of roughly 0.10% per month against a basket in which the yen is one of several components — so the mechanical SGD/JPY uplift from the July MAS move is on the order of 10–12 pips a month, not a repricing event. The BoJ, by contrast, is one meeting away from a 25bp move that would flip the pair's carry from −3bp to −28bp in a single afternoon and, more importantly, would validate a terminal-rate repricing toward the board's stated 2% neutral. On the curve the picture is already shifting: the 2-year JGB at 1.497% (touching 1.545%) against the 2-year SGS at 1.70% has compressed the Singapore front-end advantage to roughly 15–20bp from 20bp a week ago, while the 10-year JGB at 2.801% already yields 44bp more than the 10-year SGS at 2.36% — Singapore is one of only two sovereigns in the benchmarking set that Japan out-yields at ten years. The transmission into this pair is direct and unhedged: with no carry to defend a long position, spot is the only variable, and spot responds to whichever central bank has the larger step size. That is unambiguously the BoJ. The tactical window contains no MAS event and two high-information BoJ events (the 10 August Summary of Opinions and the 20 August national CPI).

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential compounds against the pair from both legs, but at different speeds and with different certainty. The BoJ leg is high-magnitude and moderately probable: three meetings (18 September, 30 October with an Outlook Report, 18 December), OIS pricing 21bp cumulative through December against a board neutral estimate of around 2%, and a live 1.25% dissent. If the BoJ delivers 50bp by end-Q1 2027, the pair's carry moves to −53bp and the two-year spread inverts decisively in Japan's favour. The MAS leg is low-magnitude and highly probable: a 1.25% slope, held or steepened again on 14 October, delivering roughly 0.3% of trade-weighted appreciation per quarter, of which only a fraction accrues against the yen specifically. The arithmetic is therefore that Singapore's policy tailwind is worth perhaps 0.6–0.9% against the yen over six months while Japan's is worth 50bp of rate convergence plus whatever terminal-rate repricing accompanies it. The offsetting consideration, and it is real, is that Japan's higher yields have repeatedly failed to support the yen in 2026 because they reflected a fiscal risk premium concentrated in the super-long rather than a policy premium in the front end — the ten-year UST-JGB spread compressed 95bp over twelve months while the yen fell 4.92%. If that pattern reasserts, this factor's transmission breaks and the pair does not fall. The observable test is whether the next JGB move is led by the 2-year or the 30-year.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential between these two economies is the widest of any pair in the benchmarking set and it points firmly the other way from the policy differential, which is why this factor nets to Neutral rather than reinforcing the bearish case. Singapore grew 5.7% year-on-year in Q2 2026 against Japan's 0.32% — a 5.4 percentage point gap — with Singapore's June NODX up 20.7% and electronics up 105.1% on the AI cycle, against a Japanese economy whose Q2 consensus is +0.80% annualised. HSBC has raised its forecast for Singapore's 2026 GDP growth to 4.6%, from 3.3%, citing continued momentum from the global artificial intelligence investment cycle alongside resilience in construction and services. If growth differentials set exchange rates, this pair would be rising. They do not set it here, because the two economies' inflation trajectories point in opposite directions and only Japan's translates into a policy instrument the market can trade. Both run core inflation at 1.6%, but Singapore's is easing while Japan's leading indicator accelerated — Tokyo July core printed 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%, and Japan's real wages rose for a sixth consecutive month in June, reinforcing the case for additional BOJ interest rate hikes. The asymmetric sensitivity is stark: Japan's 20 August national CPI can move this pair by a figure; Singapore's 23 August CPI moves it by a few pips, because MAS does not meet until October. The forces are genuinely balanced and a considered Neutral is the honest output.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the growth differential narrows mechanically and the inflation differential widens, and the two continue to offset. MTI's unchanged 2.0–4.0% full-year forecast against H1 outturns of 6.3% and 5.7% requires a sharp Singaporean deceleration by construction, and Enterprise Singapore has flagged punishing second-half base effects in the electronics series that has been carrying the economy; non-electronic exports were already contracting 2.9% in June. Japan's growth is low but stable at a 0.6% FY2026 forecast, so the gap compresses from 5.4pp toward perhaps 2–3pp by year-end without Japan doing anything. On inflation the divergence goes the other way: MAS expects Singapore's pressures to intensify from July on oil but to be contained within a 1.5–2.5% forecast, while the BoJ has raised FY2027 core to 2.4% with core-core at 2.6% and explicitly declared CPI risks skewed to the upside, and the energy-subsidy roll-off mechanically lifts Japanese measured inflation into FY2027. The bilateral transmission is that a converging growth gap removes the pair's fundamental support while a diverging inflation gap adds to the BoJ's tightening case — but the second effect is already captured in Factor 1 and double-counting it here would inflate the score. Neutral at moderate confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: SGD/JPY is a moderate-beta risk pair whose classification has been shifting, and the current regime makes it more risk-sensitive than its history suggests. The Singapore dollar is a regional safe haven backed by an AAA balance sheet and S$551.3bn of reserves, but its safe-haven property operates against Asian peers rather than against the global funding currency; the yen is the global funding currency itself. In a genuine risk-off both currencies gain against high-beta names, but the yen gains far more, so the pair falls. The relevant transmission is not equity beta but carry-trade mechanics: the yen leg carries a 185,047-contract speculative short whose covering is pair-negative, while the Singapore dollar has no speculative constituency at all. The current backdrop is superficially benign — VIX at 17.09, equities near records, credit spreads at 287bp high yield — and that would ordinarily favour the pair; but the same compression is what makes the left tail fat. Bitcoin's 52-week correlation with USD/JPY reached minus 0.90, pointing to broad US dollar strength as the likely driver rather than a mechanical carry channel, which argues the contagion risk is smaller than 2024. The pair-specific cross-asset signals to watch are the Nikkei (which has been powered by exactly the yen weakness now being fought) and the Straits Times Index at 5,628.50 near its record — both are risk-on assets, but only one of them is a direct input to its own currency's direction. On balance the asymmetry runs against the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the risk factor carries only 0.05 weight and the assessment is finely balanced, but the tail remains asymmetric against the pair. Volatility across the complex sits in the bottom decile on multiple tenors, and distributions that compressed mean-revert upward more often than downward; when they do, the yen is the highest-beta beneficiary in the G10 and the Singapore dollar is a low-beta bystander whose realised volatility of 2.83% against the dollar is the lowest in the set. The structural counter is that Singapore's own safe-haven bid is strengthening — family-office formation, corporate treasury relocation, AAA ratings, a 16.7%-of-GDP current account surplus — and that in a regional Asian stress event the Singapore dollar could outperform the yen, pushing the pair up. That is a genuine but lower-probability path. The higher-probability risk event over six months is a global carry or AI-complex unwind, in which the pair falls. Note also the degradation of the yen's own haven property: an energy-driven risk shock hits Japan's terms of trade at the same moment it triggers repatriation, and Singapore, as a refining hub, is less exposed to that specific channel. That partially offsets and is why confidence is capped at 50.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the highest-confidence factor in the analysis and the proximate reason for the tactical stance. The bilateral positioning arithmetic is exceptionally clean: the yen leg carries a combined leveraged-fund and asset-manager net short of 185,047 contracts as at the 28 July report — beyond the 150,000-contract historical extreme threshold, still growing into the high, and sitting on the second-largest open interest in CME FX — while the Singapore dollar has no listed contract and therefore no position to offset it. Net implied pair positioning is therefore long SGD/JPY at an extreme, and unlike AUD/JPY or NOK/JPY the holders of that position are not being paid to hold it: the carry is −3bp. A crowded position with no carry compensation is the most fragile configuration in FX. The squeeze catalyst has already fired twice — the BoJ's intervention on Thursday was estimated at $52.8 billion, followed by the joint operation on Friday — and the yen appreciated by nearly 5% over three sessions. The specific pair-level dynamic is that yen-cross shorts are covered indiscriminately in an official-flow event, so SGD/JPY participates fully in the covering regardless of Singapore fundamentals, which is exactly what the 30–31 July price action shows. We expect the 4 and 11 August COT reports to show the net short shrinking by 40,000–70,000 contracts, and positioning normalisation alone is worth 1.0–1.5 yen on this cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Positioning mean-reverts within weeks, so the strategic question is what the structural bilateral flow picture looks like once the squeeze is spent, and it is genuinely mixed with a mild tilt against the pair. On the pair-negative side, Japan's institutional flow architecture is turning more defensive: none of the ten major life insurers plans to increase unhedged foreign bonds, four intend to increase JGB holdings, hedge ratios are rising, and the FY2026 term-end planning assumption of USD/JPY 154 is stronger than spot — that is a standing bid for yen that activates on weakness and has no Singaporean equivalent. A gradual repatriation of Japanese capital, including a possible shift by the Government Pension Investment Fund, offers further structural support. On the pair-positive side, GPIF's announced seven-point rotation out of JGBs into foreign equities is roughly USD 52bn of structural yen selling, and Singapore's own structural inflows — family offices, treasury relocation, wealth management — create persistent SGD demand, though these are substantially offset by GIC and Temasek recycling the current-account surplus offshore. The genuinely pair-specific flow is small: bilateral direct investment is heavily one-directional, with Japan consistently one of Singapore's largest investors, cumulative FDI reaching about S$110 billion by 2014, and a documented channel in which foreign capital routes through Singapore into Japanese special-purpose vehicles investing in data centres, logistics hubs and real estate, with profits returned to Singapore as dividends. These are structural, slow-moving and not directionally decisive over six months.

That means the strategic bearish case is entirely dependent on the BoJ actually delivering, not merely threatening to.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the clearest pair-bullish factor and the reason the tactical score is not more negative. Both economies run large current-account surpluses — Singapore at 16.7% of GDP, Japan at 5.79% — but the composition and the energy exposure differ decisively. Japan's surplus is generated by primary income of ¥42.28tn that is overwhelmingly reinvested abroad and never repatriated, while its goods balance has flipped into deficit for two consecutive months (June: −¥406.9bn against a −¥120bn consensus) on record imports driven by mineral fuel purchases up 41.9% year-on-year, with terms of trade collapsing 5.0% in a single month to 83.95 against a since-1960 average of 150.50. Singapore's surplus is generated by an actual goods surplus of S$58.22bn plus services, and although its terms-of-trade index at 98.25 also sits near a record low, Singapore is a refining and petrochemical hub that captures the crack spread rather than being purely long crude exposure. Applying the framework's direction rules to a Brent price up roughly 23% on the month to $87.93: oil up is −− for JPY (Japan imports ~99% of its oil) and − for SGD (net importer but with refining offset). Net effect: the pair rises. The same logic applies to LNG — JKM up is −− for JPY and − for SGD. The transmission is real-income transfer: at current energy prices Japan is exporting national income at roughly ¥2.1tn a month while Singapore is exporting a fraction of that in net terms.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At an 0.18 strategic weight this is the single largest pair-bullish contribution and the main reason the strategic score is only mildly negative. The structural asymmetry is not cyclical: Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil and most of its gas, so every dollar of energy price is a permanent transfer of national income abroad, amplified in local-currency terms by a weak yen — which is precisely the feedback loop that has driven yen-based import prices up 29.7% year-on-year. Singapore imports crude too, but its entrepot and refining structure means it is short the level and long the spread, and its 16.7%-of-GDP surplus is large enough to absorb a terms-of-trade shock of this magnitude without approaching balance. On the creditor dimension the gap is widening in Singapore's favour: Japan has fallen to the third-largest net creditor behind Germany and China after 34 years at the top, and the yen's share of allocated global reserves fell to 5.56% in Q1 2026, while Singapore's reserves rose to S$551.3bn. On the direct bilateral relationship, the IMF DOTS data show Singapore exported $17.8bn of goods to Japan and imported $22.2bn from Japan in 2024, for a net Singapore goods deficit of $4.5bn. Japan's mirror reporting is materially different — $19.8bn of exports to Singapore against just $7.6bn of imports from Singapore, a $12.2bn Japanese surplus — and the discrepancy is characteristic of Singapore's entrepot function, where re-exports and transhipment are attributed differently by the two statistical authorities. Taking Singapore's own reporting, the structural commercial flow requires Singaporean importers to buy roughly $4.5bn of yen a year net, or about $375m a month — a persistent but trivially small pair-negative flow against daily FX turnover, and one that is dwarfed by financial flows. The trade relationship's real significance is compositional rather than directional: Japan is a major supplier of capital goods and components into Singapore's manufacturing base, so a sharp yen appreciation raises Singapore's imported input costs, which is a second-order channel through which a falling SGD/JPY feeds Singaporean core inflation and, eventually, MAS policy.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are highly credible and both have just tightened, but the guidance divergence runs against the pair on three counts: direction, frequency and sequencing. MAS communicates twice a year and delivered its message on 27 July — a second consecutive tightening, lifting the rate of appreciation of the S$NEER band very slightly while leaving the centre and width unchanged, explicitly described as smaller than April's move. That is a hawkish signal, but it is now eight days old, fully in the price, and has no follow-up until 14 October. The BoJ, by contrast, held 8-1 with Takata dissenting for 1.25% and delivered the most explicitly hawkish press conference of Ueda's governorship, and it meets on 18 September — before MAS. Sequencing matters enormously here: the BoJ sets the tone for this cross for the next ten weeks and MAS gets the last word only in mid-October. The credibility differential has also shifted materially in Japan's favour through the intervention channel, which is a new development neither dossier could fully price: Treasury Secretary Bessent confirmed the US joined Japan in coordinated intervention to counter disorderly yen movements, writing we will not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention. An official reaction function backed by two G3 treasuries is a harder constraint on yen weakness than anything MAS can deliver on the Singapore side. The counter-argument is genuine — there had been speculation the BOJ may deliver a surprise rate increase following likely coordinated intervention but that failed to materialise, and with only one dissenter, September may be off the table, with October or December looking more likely.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months guidance carries 0.12 weight and the bilateral picture becomes more balanced, because MAS's institutional advantage reasserts itself. MAS's credibility is of a stronger kind than the BoJ's: the policy instrument and the market price are the same object, so there is no transmission gap between guidance and delivery, and a steepened slope produces trade-weighted appreciation by construction rather than by persuasion. The 14 October review carries the semi-annual Macroeconomic Review, and we assess roughly a 30% probability of a third consecutive slope increase against a market that reads the July move as completing the sequence. Against that, the BoJ has three meetings, an Outlook Report, a board neutral anchor of around 2%, a hawkish dissent already at 1.25%, and now a foreign official partner. The genuine strategic risk to a bearish pair view is the Takaichi political constraint: a 352-seat LDP-Ishin supermajority elected on an expansionary platform, a Cabinet Office representative asking the Bank to act while understanding initiatives taken by the Takaichi Cabinet, and a record ¥122.3tn budget. If political pressure delays BoJ normalisation while MAS steepens again in October, this factor flips. The net remains Bearish for the pair, but at reduced confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The event calendar for this pair is grossly asymmetric: of the dated catalysts inside the tactical window with the power to move SGD/JPY by more than 20 pips, essentially all are Japanese. The 10 August Summary of Opinions, the 19 August Japanese trade balance, the 20 August national CPI and the late-August MoF intervention disclosure are all high-information; Singapore's 12 August Q2 GDP and BoP, 18 August NODX and 23 August CPI are all low-information for this cross because MAS does not meet until October and cannot respond to them. Layered on top is a one-directional official event: further intervention. That tail exists only in one direction — no authority anywhere is buying dollars against the yen — so the distribution of event outcomes for this pair is skewed downward regardless of the central expectation. Given joint action with the US is still ongoing, USD/JPY could decline below 155 if stop losses are triggered, said Moh Siong Sim of OCBC, though the success of intervention in reversing JPY weakness depends on whether intervention is complemented by or is a substitute for more hawkish BOJ stance. The one genuinely pair-bullish event channel is the Middle East: an escalation lifting Brent hurts Japan's terms of trade roughly twice as much as Singapore's, and would push the pair up even as it triggered global risk aversion. Bilateral political risk between Singapore and Japan is nil — the two are JSEPA, CPTPP and RCEP partners with no live disputes.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two dominant event channels point in opposite directions with comparable probabilities, which makes Neutral the honest reading. The pair-negative channel is BoJ normalisation combined with a repeatable, US-backed intervention function; the pair-positive channel is the unresolved Middle East situation, where a renewed Hormuz disruption raises Brent, widens Japan's goods deficit and drives its terms of trade toward the 2022 record low while Singapore's refining structure absorbs a smaller net hit. Both are live at roughly 15–20% over six months. A third channel — trade-policy escalation — is genuinely ambiguous: Singapore's entrepot economy runs total trade near three times GDP and has no domestic demand cushion, so a tariff shock hits Singapore's growth harder than Japan's, which is pair-negative; but Japan's semiconductor exposure to Section 232 action is also acute. There is one constraint worth flagging on the intervention channel: more than three interventions in six months could call Japan's IMF free-floating classification into question, so the tool has a finite number of uses inside the strategic window.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal differential between these two sovereigns is the largest of any pair in the set and it is unambiguously pair-bullish. Singapore carries Aaa from Moody's, AAA from S&P and AAA from DBRS, all stable, runs a fiscal surplus of 1.9% of GDP (improving from 0.9%), and its headline 171.3% debt ratio is an artefact of issuing SGS to invest CPF balances rather than to finance deficits — net of S$551.3bn of reserves and over USD 1tn of sovereign wealth assets the position is massively positive. Japan carries A1/A+/A, runs a record ¥122.3tn budget with debt-service costs up 10.8% on a 3.0% assumed rate that is a 29-year high, and has revised its consolidated debt estimate up to 187.6% of GDP. The market prices that gap honestly in the bond market — the 30-year JGB at 3.971% sits within 4bp of its all-time high while the 30-year SGS yields 2.46%, a 151bp premium for Japanese long duration on a three-notch-lower credit. The pair-relevant transmission is specific and well documented: a curve that steepens for fiscal rather than growth reasons is currency-negative, which is why Japanese yields rose 122bp at the ten-year over twelve months while the yen fell 4.92%. Every basis point of that premium is, mechanically, support for SGD/JPY. Tactically the offset is that the FY2026 issuance plan cut calendar-base market issuance by ¥3.8tn, which is supportive for the long end in the near term.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At 0.09 strategic weight this is the second-largest pair-bullish contribution and the arithmetic worsens for Japan over time. Japan is refinancing a 187.6%-of-GDP consolidated debt stock at progressively higher coupons every quarter while the BoJ shrinks its holdings from roughly ¥518tn to a projected ¥480tn by end-March 2027 — a withdrawal of the marginal buyer at precisely the moment supply pressure is described by the BoJ's own Summary of Opinions as at historical levels. A sitting board member has warned publicly that halting the taper risks purchases being perceived as fiscal financing. Singapore faces none of this: no financing stress, no rating action risk, no bond-market dislocation scenario, and — critically for this cross — no fiscal constraint on the durability of MAS's appreciation path. That is a second-order advantage that is rarely priced: MAS can steepen the S$NEER slope indefinitely without any possibility that a bond market forces reversal, whereas the BoJ's normalisation path is exposed to a political administration with a supermajority and an expansionary mandate. The strategic risk to this bullish reading is that it has already worked: the yen's real effective rate at an all-time low is in part the market's verdict on Japanese fiscal sustainability, so incremental deterioration may deliver diminishing pair upside. We hold this at 65 rather than higher for that reason.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The pair's own chart — not the dossiers' TWI data — has undergone a structural break. Spot at 123.081 is below the 50-day (125.173), the 100-day (124.727) and the 200-day (124.130) simultaneously, having spent essentially the entire 2026 uptrend above all three. The averages remain stacked bullishly (50>100>200), so the underlying trend is not yet dead, but the higher-highs sequence that ran 111.40 → 127.09 was broken decisively on 30 July and the 200-day has flipped from support to resistance 1.05 yen above spot. Realised volatility roughly doubled from about 7.4% on the pre-event 60-day window to approximately 12.5% over the ten sessions bracketing the intervention, then collapsed below 4% over the last five sessions — a two-day repricing followed by a base, which is the signature of a positioning event rather than a fundamental regime change. The decisive structural feature is the absence of an options market: no venue publishes an implied volatility surface, risk reversals or barrier data for SGD/JPY, which means (a) the variance risk premium cannot be measured, (b) there is no dealer gamma to dampen moves, and (c) the market has no mechanism to price the intervention tail. Liquidity is the other structural constraint — SGD/JPY is a thin cross traded almost entirely as a synthetic of USD/JPY and USD/SGD, so gap risk in a fast market is materially higher than the realised-volatility numbers suggest.

expression_assessment.directional_expression: Spot or forward is the clearly superior expression — there is no financing drag to be avoided through optionality and no observable option price against which value could be judged. Expressing a bearish-yen-cross view through SGD/JPY costs 3bp a year against 335bp in AUD/JPY and 325bp in NOK/JPY, so the position can be held through a long consolidation without bleeding. The trade-off is convexity: AUD/JPY offers far more movement per unit of view and a 14.2% valuation gap, whereas SGD/JPY offers a cleaner but smaller distribution. For a trader who wants gamma exposure to the intervention tail, the only practical route is to own USD/JPY puts — where implied volatility below 6.0 against realised of 9.58% is the cheapest optionality in the complex — and to hold the USD/SGD leg in spot, synthesising the cross. Position sizing rather than instrument selection is where the risk decision sits.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding conditions are benign and affect both legs of this cross similarly, so the factor's directional content is limited — which is why the weight is cut. The Fed balance sheet is expanding at USD 6.738tn, SOFR is stable at 3.65% against effective fed funds of 3.63%, and the broad dollar index has eased to 120.71; the dollar index fell to a seven-week low of 99.42 on 3 August following the intervention, down 1.0% over the week. Both Singapore and Japan are major offshore dollar centres and both benefit from easier dollar funding, so the net effect on the cross is close to zero. What tips the factor marginally against the pair is a genuinely new, Japan-specific development: Bessent urged the Federal Reserve to expand its Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility, which allows foreign governments to obtain US dollars using their Treasury holdings as collateral, following confirmation that the US had jointly intervened with Japan, and Bessent said the United States would consider increasing the size of the Federal Reserve's repurchase facility in coming months. That is a dedicated dollar-liquidity backstop for the Japanese official sector specifically. It reduces the risk that intervention forces Japanese Treasury sales, extends the MoF's operational firepower, and has no Singaporean equivalent — a small but unambiguous pair-negative asymmetry. The material limitation is that neither the JPY/USD nor any SGD/USD cross-currency basis was obtainable from any public source, so the most sensitive early-warning indicator for this factor is missing on both legs.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the dollar channel is genuinely two-sided for this cross and the honest reading is Neutral. Both currencies' short rates are, to different degrees, endogenous to US conditions: Singapore's SORA is mechanically set by covered interest parity against the dollar given the band, and Japan's institutional sector is among the world's largest dollar borrowers whose hedged-asset economics turn on the basis. A Fed that resumes hiking widens the SOFR-SORA gap beyond 268bp and pressures the Singapore dollar through the funding channel, while simultaneously widening the Fed-BoJ gap and pressuring the yen — the two effects broadly cancel in the cross. The 31 December year-end funding turn reliably widens cross-currency basis and creates a temporary dollar bid; historically that hits the yen harder than the Singapore dollar, so it is a modest pair-positive seasonal inside the window. Against that, the FIMA expansion is a structural, Japan-specific improvement. With the basis unobservable on both legs and the two channels offsetting, no directional stance is defensible.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of −0.3637 on a −1.00 to +1.00 scale is a firm bearish reading for the pair, produced by seven negative contributions against two positives. Policy & Rates alone supplies 40% of the gross negative at −0.1440, with Flows & Positioning at −0.0744 and Guidance at −0.0434 next. The positives are concentrated in the two structural factors — External Balance at +0.0330 and Fiscal at +0.0232 — which together offset only 15% of the negative block at tactical weights. Mapping: below 0.05 → conviction 1; 0.05–0.15 → 2; 0.15–0.30 → 3; 0.30–0.45 → 4; above 0.45 → 5. −0.3637 maps to conviction 4.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the factors that dominate are Policy & Rates at 0.24 and Flows & Positioning at 0.12, and both point the same way for a specific bilateral reason: this pair has no carry to defend a long position and no Singaporean catalyst to support it inside the window, while the yen leg carries the most extreme speculative short in the complex and a central bank one meeting from a hike. The weighted score of −0.3637 is built on seven negative contributions totalling −0.4199 against just two positives worth +0.0562, and the concentration matters — Policy & Rates, Guidance and Event Risk are all expressions of the same underlying fact, which is that the BoJ meets on 18 September while MAS does not meet until 14 October. The two standalone dossiers reinforce rather than conflict once the arithmetic is done: both are bullish their own currency, but the JPY dossier expects 4.11% appreciation over six months against the SGD dossier's 1.7%, and mechanically combining their six-month targets gives SGD/JPY at 120.63 — a 2.0% fall that neither dossier states because neither is looking at this cross. The bilateral factor that modifies both standalone views is the carry structure: at −3bp this is the only carry-neutral yen cross, which means the pair moves on relative policy trajectory alone with no yield cushion in either direction, and it means a short position costs essentially nothing to hold. What is priced versus what we expect diverges in one identifiable place: spot at 123.08 and a six-month forward at 122.74 embed a continuation of the pre-intervention regime and a September BoJ hike probability nearer 30% than 44%, while a leading Japanese bond strategist has described a September hike as a done deal and the official reaction function has been hardened by US participation. The path of least resistance is lower: the pair has broken below all three moving averages, the 200-day at 124.13 has flipped to resistance, and the intervention tail is one-directional. The dated catalysts inside the window are the 7 August US payrolls (consensus 91K), the 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions, the 20 August Japanese national CPI and the late-August MoF intervention disclosure, none of which has a Singaporean counterweight. Conviction is 4 rather than 5 because the two structural pair-bullish factors — a 10.9pp current-account gap and a three-notch sovereign-rating gap — are genuine and permanent, because the pair has already moved 3.15% before we act, and because a reclaim of 124.13 would neutralise the technical case without any new information.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among yen crosses, SGD/JPY ranks 4th most attractive short of the eight in the set, behind AUD/JPY, NOK/JPY and NZD/JPY. It loses to AUD/JPY because that cross combines a 335bp carry, a 14.2% valuation gap and the highest risk beta in G10 FX — more convexity per unit of view, at the cost of carry. It loses to NOK/JPY because Norway is the direct beneficiary of the same energy shock that is destroying Japan's terms of trade, making that the cleanest expression of the structural yen problem. It beats EUR/JPY, GBP/JPY, CAD/JPY and CHF/JPY on cost of carry: at −3bp SGD/JPY is by far the cheapest yen cross to be short. Among SGD crosses, SGD/JPY ranks 1st most attractive short of the seven — it is the only SGD cross where the counterparty currency has an actively hiking central bank plus a US-backed official bid. The honest summary is that this is the cheapest short-yen-cross expression available, not the highest-conviction one.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of −0.1051 is a mildly bearish reading, less than a third of the tactical magnitude, and the gap is almost entirely a weight-reallocation effect rather than a change of view. Only three stances change between horizons (Event Risk and USD Liquidity fall to Neutral, all others hold direction), but External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.18 of weight, taking its contribution from +0.0330 to +0.1116, and Fiscal from 0.04 to 0.09, taking its from +0.0232 to +0.0585. Those two reweightings alone add +0.114 to the score. −0.1051 maps to conviction 2. This is a directional view held with genuine humility: the cyclical case against the pair is strong and the structural case for it is also strong.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the picture changes materially because External Balance rises to 0.18 and Fiscal to 0.09, and both are unambiguously pair-bullish. Singapore runs a current-account surplus of 16.7% of GDP against Japan's 5.79%, carries Aaa/AAA/AAA against A1/A+/A, runs a fiscal surplus of 1.9% of GDP against a record ¥122.3tn budget, and holds S$551.3bn of reserves plus over USD 1tn of sovereign wealth against a Japanese sovereign refinancing 187.6% of GDP at a 29-year-high assumed rate with a shrinking central bank bid. Those two factors together contribute +0.1701, and they are the reason a cross that looks tactically obvious is strategically a low-conviction call. Policy & Rates remains the largest single contribution at −0.1392, because Japan is the only economy in the pair with 100bp of latent tightening against its own central bank's neutral estimate while Singapore's policy tightening is capped at a 1.25% annual trade-weighted slope of which only a fraction accrues against the yen. Guidance adds −0.0672 on the meeting sequence and the US-backed official reaction function. The dossiers interact in a way that neither states: both are bullish, but the yen's expected appreciation is 2.4 times Singapore's, so combining their own six-month targets gives 120.63 on this cross. The bilateral factor that modifies both is energy — the framework's direction rules make oil ↑ doubly negative for the yen and singly negative for the Singapore dollar, so any escalation in the unresolved Middle East situation is pair-bullish and cuts directly against the strategic short. What is priced versus what we expect: the six-month forward at 122.74 embeds a 0.55% annualised SGD depreciation, essentially one BoJ hike and nothing else, while retail model forecasters cluster at 125–128 for late 2026; we expect 121.00, which is below the forward and well below the model consensus but above the 120.63 the two dossiers mechanically imply, the difference being our 30% probability on a third MAS slope increase on 14 October. The path of least resistance is a slow drift lower punctuated by two binary events — 18 September and 14 October — with long flat stretches between them. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the structural pair-bullish block is genuinely powerful, because the pair has no carry to compensate for a long holding period, and because the 2026 precedent in which Japanese yields rose without helping the yen has not been falsified.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically SGD/JPY ranks 6th most attractive short among the eight yen crosses, falling two places from its tactical ranking. It loses to AUD/JPY and NOK/JPY for the same reasons as tactically, and additionally to EUR/JPY and GBP/JPY, both of which pair a hawkish or neutral counterparty against the yen without carrying Singapore's offsetting structural strengths — the euro area does not run a 16.7%-of-GDP surplus and does not carry a AAA rating with a net-positive sovereign balance sheet. It still beats CHF/JPY (where the yen out-yields the franc by 100bp and the SNB is intervening against its own currency) and CAD/JPY (where Canada is contracting with core inflation below target). Among SGD crosses, SGD/JPY falls to 3rd most attractive short strategically, behind short SGD/NOK and short SGD/AUD, because over a longer horizon Singapore's structural advantages — the surplus, the ratings, the reserves — assert themselves more strongly against the yen than against the high-carry surplus currencies. The ranking would improve to 2nd among yen crosses on a single condition: a 25bp BoJ hike on 18 September accompanied by guidance pointing explicitly at the 2% neutral rate.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons are aligned in direction but sharply divergent in magnitude. The divergence is mechanical rather than analytical — only two stances change (Event Risk and USD Liquidity fall to Neutral) and none reverses. What changes is weight: External Balance triples from 0.06 to 0.18 and Fiscal more than doubles from 0.04 to 0.09, adding +0.114 to the score, while Inflation & Growth halves from 0.18 to 0.10 and Flows from 0.12 to 0.06. In plain terms, the tactical case rests on positioning, meeting sequence and a broken chart, all of which carry heavy short-horizon weight; the strategic case has to survive a 10.9pp current-account gap and a three-notch rating gap, both of which carry heavy long-horizon weight and both of which favour the pair.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: 18 September 2026 (BoJ meeting), with 14 October 2026 (MAS review) as the confirming or contradicting event. If the BoJ hikes and MAS holds, the two horizons converge and strategic conviction rises to 3 or 4; if the BoJ holds through October and MAS steepens a third time, the tactical case will have expired as a completed squeeze and the strategic case flips to mildly bullish.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Size the tactical view larger than the strategic view and treat the strategic position as an option on the September meeting rather than as a structural holding. The near-zero carry makes that unusually cheap to do — a position can be held from now through both events for less than 2 pips of financing — but the strategic risk/reward of 0.61:1 on central cases argues against sizing the longer-horizon expression as though it carried the tactical conviction.

signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the only rate-expectation series that moves this cross, because Singapore has no policy rate to price — the entire relative-policy component of SGD/JPY is a one-sided function of BoJ pricing, which is not true of any SGD cross against a conventional inflation-targeting central bank.

signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's cleanest test of which Japanese yield regime is operating. Because Singapore is one of only two sovereigns Japan out-yields at ten years, the spread between JGBs and SGS is unusually informative — a widening led by the long end is pair-bullish (fiscal premium), a widening led by the front end is pair-bearish (policy premium).

assumptions: The 390-day Twelve Data OHLC series is treated as the source of truth for spot (123.081, 6 August close), the 52-week range (111.403–127.089), the range percentile (74), the moving averages (50d 125.173, 100d 124.727, 200d 124.130) and the performance figures (1M −2.19%, 3M −1.43%, 6M −0.99%, 1Y +3.93%). The supplied performance figures do not reconcile exactly with point-to-point calculations from the OHLC series on either a 6 August or a 1 August anchor — they appear to be calendar-anchored on a provider convention that could not be reproduced — and where narrative precision was required the price action was described directly from the OHLC rather than relying on the aggregate figures.
Realised volatility estimates are computed from the daily closes on a log-return basis annualised at √252 and are stated as approximations.

There is a five-day gap between the stated valuation date (2026-08-01) and the last price observation (2026-08-06). The 6 August close was used as spot per the framework's source-of-truth rule, and web-researched developments through 6 August — principally the confirmation of joint US-Japan intervention — were incorporated because excluding them would have produced a materially misleading picture of the pair's driver set. Dossier data remains as at the 2026-08-01 valuation date.

No implied volatility surface, risk reversal, vol term structure, barrier data or option open-interest data exists in any publicly retrievable form for SGD/JPY. This is a compound gap: neither USD/SGD nor SGD/JPY options are publicly quoted, meaning the variance risk premium, the IV percentile and the option-implied event premium for this cross are unmeasurable, not merely unmeasured. No values have been estimated or asserted beyond an explicitly flagged proxy inference of 9–10 fair implied volatility, which is not used in any scoring.

Forward points are derived, not quoted. There is no publicly retrievable SGD/JPY forward curve, so the 1M, 3M and 6M points have been constructed by crossing the two dossiers' own USD-leg forward outrights and rebasing the resulting percentage to the current spot. A parallel construction from raw covered interest parity on SORA and the BoJ target gives materially smaller points (−0.3/−0.9/−1.8 pips versus −4.9/−14.8/−34.5 pips); the difference is cross-currency basis and bill-yield spread on the yen leg, and both constructions are disclosed rather than reconciled. The cross-currency basis itself was unobtainable for either leg, which caps Factor 10 confidence at 50 on both horizons.

Support and resistance levels are a hybrid. The levels at 122.43–122.46, 121.29, 120.34–120.47, 123.46 and 126.30–127.09 are derived directly from the OHLC series (session highs and lows), and the 124.130, 124.727 and 125.173 levels are the supplied moving averages. Public technical coverage of SGD/JPY is extremely thin, so the two levels sourced from web research (120.9 and 116.3) are mapped from USD/JPY levels published by third parties, using a USD/SGD of 1.282, and are labelled as such. That mapping assumes a stable USD/SGD, which is reasonable given 2.83% realised volatility but is nonetheless an approximation.

Bilateral trade figures are taken directly from the injected IMF DOTS block and have not been re-estimated from the web. The material mirror discrepancy between Singapore's and Japan's reporting ($4.5bn Singapore deficit versus $12.2bn Japanese surplus) is disclosed and attributed to entrepot re-export accounting; Singapore's reporting was used for the flow calculation and the alternative is flagged.

Weight adjustments total ±0.04 on the tactical horizon and ±0.04 on the strategic, all within the ±0.05 per-factor limit, and both sets sum to exactly 1.00. The largest single adjustment is the −0.04 reduction to Factor 10 on both horizons, justified by the non-USD-cross rule in the framework's adjustment patterns.

The 30% probability assigned to a third MAS slope increase on 14 October is inherited from the SGD dossier and is that dossier's own assessment, not a market-implied figure — no instrument prices MAS band decisions. The September BoJ hike probability is taken from published market sources and the material dispersion between them (44% per LSEG against a competing view that September is off the table) is reported rather than resolved; that dispersion is the explicit reason Factor 1 tactical confidence sits at 60 rather than higher.

Both dossiers carry their own extensive disclosed limitations — no CFTC data for SGD, contested USD/SGD moving averages, corrected Brent levels, an inferred rather than confirmed intervention size, and unobtainable cross-currency basis — and those limitations propagate into this analysis. Where a dossier flagged a figure as estimated or contested, the flag was carried forward rather than presenting it as established.
